# Supply Chain & Inventory Analytics Dashboard

A Streamlit dashboard and a pandas notebook for a made-up distributor, **Meridian Distribution Co.**, that buys from 21 suppliers, stocks 200 products in three warehouses and ships to customers. It covers January 2024 to December 2025, with a stock snapshot taken on 31 December 2025.

**Every number in this repository is synthetic.** The company, suppliers and data were generated by `scripts/generate_data.py` for portfolio use. Nothing here describes a real business.

Built with Python, pandas, NumPy, Plotly, Streamlit and Jupyter. It runs offline once the packages are installed: no API keys, no database.

## The questions it answers

- Which products hold the most inventory value, and which are at or below reorder point?
- How much is being ordered, from whom, and how concentrated is that spend?
- Which suppliers deliver late, and is the evidence strong enough to say so?
- Which categories and products drive demand, and when?
- Which products have far more stock than their sales justify?

> **Screenshot:** none is committed yet, because a screenshot has to come from the running app. Start the dashboard, capture a tab, save it as `assets/dashboard_preview.png`, and link it here.

## Reading the charts

The charts were chosen to show a comparison or a risk, not just a total.

| Chart | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Inventory value treemap | Tiles are products, sized by value and coloured by stock status. A red or amber tile that is also large is money at risk. |
| Top 10 by inventory value | Bars are coloured by stock status; the label gives the cumulative share of total inventory value. |
| Stock status by category | 100% stacked bars, riskiest category first. Totals hide which category the low stock sits in. |
| Warehouse by category heatmap | Where value is concentrated; units per warehouse are in the row labels. |
| Monthly procurement spend | Stacked by category with a 3-month average, so a spike can be traced to a category. |
| Spend by supplier (Pareto) | Bars plus a cumulative line. The subtitle states how many suppliers account for 80% of ordered value. |
| Purchase order status by quarter | Shows open and overdue orders accumulating in the most recent quarters. |
| On-time rate with 95% ranges | Each supplier has only 17 to 35 orders, so a rate alone overstates certainty. The line is a Wilson 95% interval, and `n` is in the label. |
| Lead time box plots | Spread, not just the average. The diamond is the lead time the supplier quotes, so you can see when quotes are optimistic. |
| Delay matrix | Share of orders late (x) against how late they are when late (y), sized by spend. Top right means frequent and long. |
| Stock-out trend | Monthly units with a 3-month average and a fitted linear trend. |
| Top 10 dispatched | Coloured by category; the label gives the number of dispatches. |
| Stock cover vs demand | Months of cover against dispatch rate on log axes. Products above the 12-month line are the slow movers. |
| Demand seasonality heatmap | Each category's average month divided by its own average, so 1.30 means 30% above a typical month. |

## Decisions worth knowing about

**Procurement spend is ordered value, not cash paid.** There are no invoices in the data, so the honest definition is quantity ordered x unit cost, excluding cancelled orders. The same definition is used on every tab and in the scorecard.

**Snapshot and period metrics are separated in the layout.** The KPI strip has a teal band for figures that describe the stock position on 31 December 2025 and a navy band for figures that depend on the date range. Inventory value and low-stock counts do not change when you move the date filter, because only one snapshot exists. Pretending otherwise would mean inventing historical balances.

**Delivery metrics count purchase orders, not lines.** A PO is delivered as a whole, so counting lines would let a 4-line order count four times.

**The supplier flag is deliberately simple.** Below 75% on time is "Needs review", below the overall rate is "Below average", fewer than 5 completed orders is "Low volume". The interval on the chart is there so the flag is not read as more precise than it is.

**Suggested reorder quantity is a rule, not a forecast.** For low and out-of-stock products it brings stock up to 2 x reorder point, rounded up to a multiple of 5.

**Slow-moving means more than 12 months of cover**, using the average dispatch rate in the selected period, or no dispatches at all.

## What the generated data shows

| | Result |
|---|---|
| Inventory value | About $165,700. Tools & Hardware holds the most (about $50,800, 31%). |
| Stock risk | 24 of 200 products (12.0%) are at or below reorder point; 11 have no stock. |
| Procurement | About $1.24 million ordered. Kestrel Fasteners is largest at about $142,100 (11%). |
| Delivery | 82.1% on time overall, 18.6 days average lead time. 10 of 21 suppliers are below the overall rate; four are under 75%, the lowest being Cobalt Peak Electronics at 54.5%. |
| Demand | Packaging Materials ships the most units (23%) and peaks in November and December. Monthly dispatches trend upward across the two years. |
| Slow-moving stock | 31 products tie up about $55,000, a third of inventory value. |

Because the data is generated, these figures show that the analysis works. They are not benchmarks.

What I would do with results like these: reorder the out-of-stock items first; ask the four low-rate suppliers whether delays are one-offs or a pattern and whether their quoted lead times are realistic; check the slow-moving list before the next purchase cycle; and watch the few suppliers that account for most spend, since their delays cost the most.

## Data

Files in `data/`, produced with a fixed seed so regenerating gives identical output.

| File | Rows | Contents |
|---|---:|---|
| `products.csv` | 200 | Category, supplier, cost, price, reorder point, safety stock, current stock, warehouse |
| `suppliers.csv` | 21 | Region, category supplied, quoted lead time, contact status |
| `purchase_orders.csv` | 1,267 | PO lines (534 orders) with expected and actual delivery dates, status, quantity received |
| `inventory_movements.csv` | 4,593 | Stock In, Stock Out and Adjustment movements |
| `opening_balances.csv` | 200 | Stock on hand at the start of 2024 |

`opening_balances.csv` and `Quantity_Received` go beyond the minimum schema. They exist so current stock can be checked exactly.

```
suppliers ──< products ──< purchase_orders >── suppliers
                 ├──< inventory_movements
                 └── opening_balances
```

Stock follows one identity:

```
Current_Stock = Opening_Stock + Stock In - Stock Out + Adjustments
```

Stock In rows come only from received PO lines, one per line, dated on the actual delivery date and carrying the `PO_Line_ID`, so a delivery cannot be counted twice. A dispatch is capped at the stock on hand, so balances never go negative.

Delivery status follows the dates: *Delivered On Time*, *Delivered Late*, *In Transit* (not yet due on 31 Dec 2025), *Overdue* (due earlier, not received) or *Cancelled*.

**A bug the charts caught.** My first generator balanced stock by adding extra dispatches in the last quarter of 2025. The monthly dispatch chart showed demand tripling at the end, which was not real. The balancing dispatches are now spread over all 24 months, and `validate_data.py` still passes either way, which is a reminder that integrity checks do not catch a misleading pattern.

## KPI definitions

| KPI | Definition | Depends on date range? |
|---|---|---|
| Total Inventory Value | Current stock x unit cost | No (snapshot) |
| Low-Stock Products | Current stock at or below reorder point, including out of stock | No (snapshot) |
| Total Procurement Spend | Ordered value of PO lines, excluding cancelled | Yes, by order date |
| Active Products | Products with at least one stock movement | Yes, by movement date |
| Supplier On-Time Delivery Rate | On-time completed POs / completed POs x 100 | Yes, by order date |
| Average Supplier Lead Time | Mean days from order date to actual receipt, completed POs | Yes, by order date |

Stock status: Out of Stock is 0 units, Low Stock is above 0 and at or below reorder point, Healthy Stock is above it. Rates show "n/a" when nothing has been delivered.

## Running it

Python 3.10 or newer.

```bash
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
streamlit run app.py
```

Open the URL Streamlit prints, usually http://localhost:8501.

**Windows (PowerShell, from the project folder):**

```powershell
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
streamlit run app.py
```

If PowerShell refuses to run the activation script, run `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass` first.

**GitHub Codespaces:** create a codespace from the repository; the dev container installs the requirements. Run `streamlit run app.py` in the terminal, open the **Ports** tab, and open port 8501 (labelled *Streamlit dashboard*) in the browser.

**Notebook:** open `notebooks/supply_chain_analysis.ipynb` in VS Code or Jupyter and run it top to bottom. It uses `../data`, so leave it in `notebooks/`. Saved outputs are included.

**Regenerate and check the data:**

```bash
python scripts/generate_data.py
python scripts/validate_data.py
```

`validate_data.py` runs 53 checks: keys and relationships, PO totals, delivery-status logic, receipts counted once, stock reconciliation, no negative balances, and agreement between the KPI functions and independent calculations.

## Project layout

```
app.py                     dashboard
src/inventory_analysis.py  stock status, cover, seasonality, demand helpers
src/supplier_analysis.py   spend, delivery metrics, scorecard, Wilson intervals
scripts/generate_data.py   seeded synthetic data generator
scripts/validate_data.py   integrity and KPI checks
notebooks/                 step-by-step analysis with outputs
data/                      the five CSV files
assets/                    logo (SVG and PNG)
.streamlit/config.toml     theme
.devcontainer/             Codespaces setup
```

## Limitations

- The data is generated. Seasonality, supplier reliability and stock levels come from rules in the generator.
- Only one stock snapshot exists, so there is no historical inventory value.
- Spend is ordered value. Deliveries are always complete: no short shipments, returns or invoices.
- Inventory is valued at current unit cost, not batch cost.
- Reorder suggestions and the slow-moving test are simple rules with no demand forecasting.
- Suppliers have few orders each, which is why the on-time chart shows intervals.
- Amounts are in dollars with no currency modelling.
